title: Amid War and Energy Crisis, Over 1.5 Million Begin Hajj Pilgrimage
summary: The annual Hajj pilgrimage, a cornerstone of the Islamic faith, commenced in Saudi Arabia on Monday with over 1.5 million pilgrims from abroad already in the kingdom, according to Hajj passport forces commander Saleh bin Saad al-Murabba. The massive gathering takes place under the shadow of a fragile ceasefire in the Iran war and a global energy crisis that has roiled economies worldwide. For many, the journey is the fulfillment of a lifelong spiritual obligation. "I am in a state of blessing and happiness," said Egyptian pilgrim Samya Abdul Moneim in Mecca. "It's an indescribable feeling, truly." The Hajj, required once in a lifetime for every Muslim who is physically and financially able, is both physically grueling and deeply transformative. Pilgrims have been circling the Kaaba in the Grand Mosque amid sweltering heat, shielding themselves with umbrellas and handheld fans as volunteers distribute water and operate misting fans. "This Hajj is, in effect, a hard reset for me," said Youssef Chouhoud, a political scientist from the United States, speaking from the tent city of Mina. "It is for many pilgrims the most difficult thing they will ever do in their lives. But nothing this meaningful is ever going to be easy." He noted the spirit of cooperation, with pilgrims "competing with one another in giving charity and helping each other along the way." The pilgrimage's spiritual climax arrives on Tuesday at the plain of Arafat, where worshippers will stand in prayer, seek forgiveness, and remember loved ones. The rituals unfold as the U.S., Iran, and regional allies discuss a memorandum of understanding that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz and ease the energy crunch triggered by recent conflicts. Despite the uncertainty, pilgrims say their faith sustains them.
why_it_matters: Hajj is not just a religious ritual; it is one of the largest annual gatherings on Earth, and its smooth running depends on global stability. When war and energy crises threaten, they can affect everything from travel costs to safety. Understanding how faith and world events intersect helps teens see that local actions often ripple across continents—and that even a teenager’s awareness of geopolitical chokepoints like the Strait of Hormuz can shed light on why petrol prices at home might spike.

background_read: Hajj is one of the Five Pillars of Islam and a religious duty for every Muslim who is physically and financially able to make the journey. It takes place during the Islamic lunar month of Dhu al-Hijjah, and its rituals reenact events in the life of the Prophet Muhammad and earlier prophets.

Pilgrims circle the Kaaba (the black cube in Mecca’s Grand Mosque, the direction Muslims face during daily prayers) seven times. They then travel to the tent city of Mina (a vast temporary camp of white tents outside Mecca that houses millions during Hajj) and later spend a day of intense prayer at Arafat (the plain where Prophet Muhammad gave his farewell sermon).

This year’s pilgrimage is overshadowed by a fragile ceasefire in the Iran war and a global energy crisis. The Strait of Hormuz (a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which about one-fifth of the world’s oil passes) has been a flashpoint; any disruption there sends fuel prices soaring worldwide. Saleh bin Saad al-Murabba (the Saudi commander responsible for Hajj passport control) confirmed the huge numbers.

Discussions between the U.S., Iran and regional allies on a memorandum of understanding could reopen the strait and ease the energy crunch, but the situation remains uncertain. For pilgrims, however, the focus remains spiritual. Historically, Hajj has continued through wars and famines, a testament to its enduring pull on the faithful.

perspectives.description: For the pilgrims, completing Hajj brings immense spiritual fulfillment and a sense of global Muslim unity. The spirit of cooperation—competing to give charity and help each other—shows how hardship can bring out the best in people, and the massive mobilisation of volunteers and authorities demonstrates impressive faith-based logistics.

The sheer number of pilgrims in extreme heat creates serious health and safety risks, and past Hajjs have seen deadly stampedes. Critics also worry that the fragile ceasefire could collapse during the pilgrimage, leaving millions stranded or caught up in regional tensions; the energy crisis makes the journey even costlier, potentially excluding the poorest believers.

Hajj acts as a mirror for global interdependence: a war in Iran, a chokepoint in the Gulf, and the energy crisis all intersect with a purely spiritual event. This reveals how religion, politics and economics are never fully separate, and how Saudi Arabia’s management of Hajj is both a religious duty and a geopolitical tool that influences its standing among Muslim nations.

If the memorandum of understanding on the Strait of Hormuz is signed, it could reduce energy costs and stabilise the region, making future pilgrimages more affordable and safe. Better crowd management, climate-adjusted rituals and greater international cooperation might become permanent improvements, safeguarding Hajj for coming generations even as conflicts evolve.
